title: Friend betrayals & breakups: horror stories & advice
summary: A mailbag episode on platonic friendship: why friendships are for seasons and reasons, how to build community as an adult by saying yes to bids and hosting recurring events, the value of opposite-sex friendships and group trips, and why friendship breakups hurt more than romantic ones. Cherie walks through the Stanford GSB Interpersonal Dynamics ('Touchy Feely') repair framework of observed behavior, feelings and not crossing the net.

ideas.idea: Friendships are for different seasons and different reasons; expecting them all to be evergreen sets you up for disappointment.
ideas.detail: Jean's biggest lesson from 35 years: you and your best friend from ten years ago are both different people, so unless you grow in parallel you will not be friends in the same way, and that is okay. The sisters lost touch with childhood friends after moving from Long Island to California.

ideas.idea: Choose close friends you genuinely respect in at least one specific way, because you are the product of the five people closest to you.
ideas.detail: Jean's closest girlfriends are mostly HBS classmates she never really knew during school (a class of about 1,000); she recommends asking whether there is one thing you respect and learn from in each friend. Since a romantic partner is only one of the five, platonic friends arguably matter more.

ideas.idea: When building community in a new city, say yes to invitations, especially the first or second time someone reaches out.
ideas.detail: Cherie's friend Eric taught her that if you decline early bids people stop thinking to invite you; in Stanford GSB language, meet people's 'bids' for connection. Once established you can be pickier.

ideas.idea: Create recurring events around your own interests; consistency is what turns acquaintances into community.
ideas.detail: Jean's Bachelorette watch party became a 7-plus-year book club that is the cornerstone of her LA community; Cherie hosted weekly Monday poker nights with a core four women at Stanford. A recurring calendar hold gives everyone something to look forward to when life gets busy.

ideas.idea: Back-channel before proposing group plans so someone endorses immediately and creates momentum.
ideas.detail: Cherie learned from a work mentor that big executive meetings require back-channeling ahead of time, then applied it to group chats: line up a 'yes person' privately, propose the plan publicly, and have them heart it right away to avoid five hours of crickets.

ideas.idea: Platonic friendships with the opposite sex bring different perspectives and, in practice, better access to investment deal flow.
ideas.detail: Cherie's guy friends up-level her on personal finance; Jean says most of her unique investing opportunities came through male friend groups, and she is trying to change that with her fund Sunbird Ventures by getting women to share deals intentionally.

ideas.idea: Group trips and novel shared experiences deepen friendships and romantic relationships alike.
ideas.detail: Traveling shows different sides of people, and experiencing something for the first time together creates a serotonin spike; Jean notes The Bachelor engineers skydiving and bungee dates for exactly this reason. Cherie tries to plan a new group experience intentionally every year.

ideas.idea: To make a friend, act as if the person is already your friend and do not feel embarrassed about reaching out too much.
ideas.detail: From a Washington Post article ('Would you be mine? Could you be mine? Won't you be my friend?'); Jean recognized people who had done this to her and it worked through assumed familiarity and multiple points of contact.

ideas.idea: Friendship breakups are more painful than romantic ones because you invest for years and never anticipate an ending, and most people avoid closure.
ideas.detail: Citing a New York Magazine/The Cut article, most friendship breakups are not clean and get no conversation; both sisters' most painful breakups were in college when neither party had the vocabulary or courage to address the hurt.

ideas.idea: A friendship breakup is usually not about you; look at what is going on in the other person's life and whether it is their pattern.
ideas.detail: Jean says the 'it's not you, it's me' trope is actually true for many friendship endings, and though it is hard to remember in the moment, it is what she would tell anyone going through one.

ideas.idea: Stop expecting friends to show up exactly the way you do; adjust expectations per person rather than holding everyone to your own standard.
ideas.detail: Jean, deeply loyal and conscientious, used to be hurt by flakes until a friend showed her she double-books plans with a chronically canceling friend and stays unoffended. Friends for different reasons means a fun event friend need not be a dinner-with-parents friend.

ideas.idea: When people tell you who they are (e.g., how they split bills), temper your own behavior to match, or resentment builds and becomes conflict.
ideas.detail: A friend who Venmo-charges $4.55 for a split Uber is signaling they are stringent; if Jean kept treating expecting reciprocity that never comes, she would set herself up for disappointment. Unresolved resentment is the root of friendship conflict, and money comes up in every friendship.

ideas.idea: Be selective about where your genuine energy goes and look for reciprocity, especially as you get older.
ideas.detail: Cherie was less discerning in college but now gives deep care only to friends where love and care flow both ways, since one-sided 100% effort friendships are draining.

ideas.idea: Stanford GSB's Interpersonal Dynamics ('Touchy Feely') teaches a repair vocabulary: share observed behavior and how it made you feel, and never 'cross the net' to assume intent.
ideas.detail: The course puts about 12 people in an unstructured T-group where people comment on how others' disclosures landed; people cry, it is ranked first, and skipping it is questioned. Because Cherie's friends took the same class, they share a language for making up after conflict.

ideas.idea: Repairing a friendship follows steps: commit to talk, state the observed behavior, say how it made you feel, listen and acknowledge, then commit to a way forward.
ideas.detail: The approached party must receive the bid, confirm or deny intent, and acknowledge the hurt even if they disagree; you can also request a specific behavior change. Repair of lost trust may take many conversations and changed behaviors, not one 45-minute talk.

ideas.idea: Use a feelings chart to label emotions precisely, because you cannot discuss a feeling you cannot name.
ideas.detail: Cherie keeps a feelings chart (like Hoffman's feeling list, 50-plus words) above her desk and suggests both parties can bring it into a repair conversation. She recently had tearful repair conversations with two close friends and the friendships came out stronger.

ideas.idea: Never use attacking language or assume another person's intent; you have no idea what is going on with them.
ideas.detail: Example: a coworker, Jason, does not wave back on the street; instead of spiraling to 'Jason hates me', ask him and learn he was lost in thought after a meeting. This mindset helped Cherie let go because it is hardly ever about her.

ideas.idea: Swallowing a grievance is the short-term easy path, but it breeds resentment and growing distance.
ideas.detail: Despite being conflict-avoidant, Cherie set aside time to talk through friction with close friends; part of repair is also not harboring resentment afterward.
